content.text:
**Short answer:** Don't accept it as-is, and don't walk away. It's a reasonable opening offer: it pays a lot more in year 1, but averaged over four years it's only a little better than staying at Meta. You're happy where you are, which gives you leverage. Negotiate.

## First, check the vesting schedule

How the $1.08M vests changes the picture, so ask the recruiter for the schedule in writing.
As of 2026, almost all (99%) of Google's offers follow the 38/32/20/10 GSU vesting structure
, which means 38% in year 1, 32% in year 2, 20% in year 3 and 10% in year 4. That said,
Google has experimented with quite a few vesting schedules over the past few years

, so confirm yours.

## What the offer is worth, assuming 38/32/20/10 and no refreshes

| | Base + bonus | Stock | **Total** | Meta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Year 1 | $282K | $410K | **$692K** | ~$476K (you said $200K vests in the next 12 months) |
| Year 2 | $282K | $346K | **$628K** | ~$526K |
| Year 3 | $282K | $216K | **$498K** | ~$526K |
| Year 4 | $282K | $108K | **$390K** | ~$526K |
| **4-year average** | | | **~$552K** | **~$526K** |

What this shows:
- **Over four years, Google pays only about $26K/yr more.** Most of the gain comes early. By years 3–4 you'd earn less than at Meta unless Google's refreshes fill the gap, and the recruiter said those aren't guaranteed.
- **Meta also gives refreshes**, so "refreshes stack" isn't an advantage unique to Google. Your Meta refreshes are already vesting, while Google's would start from zero.
- **The offer is below typical pay for this level.** Levels.fyi shows Google L6 Product Managers at about

median total comp. Your offer is about $552K.
- **The base is mid-range, and $5K below what you make now.** The posted range goes up to $271K, so there's room.
- **Watch your Meta bonus timing.** If you leave before Meta pays its annual bonus, you'll probably lose that ~$36K. You also give up all your unvested Meta stock.
- **The bonus percentage is fixed.** The 20% target is set by level and generally can't be negotiated, so don't spend effort there.

## What to ask for

| Item | Current | Ask | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Base** | $235K | **$260K** | It's below your current base, and the posted range reaches $271K |
| **Stock (GSUs)** | $1.08M | **$1.35M** (+25%) | Brings you closer to the ~$600K level median and protects years 3–4 |
| **Sign-on bonus** | $0 | **$100K** (could be split across years 1 and 2) | Covers the Meta bonus and stock you'd give up |

Expect to settle somewhere in between, for example about $250K base, $1.25M in stock and a $50–75K sign-on. Sign-on is usually the easiest item to get. Recruiters say
sign-on bonuses at L6 are also meaningful, often $50,000 to $100,000, and sit in a separate budget that does not require the same approval chain

as raises to base or stock. If they won't move on base, push harder on stock and sign-on.

## Sample script

> "Thanks, I'm excited about the role. To be candid, I wasn't looking and I'm happy at Meta. As it stands, this offer pays me less in base than I make today, and over four years it's roughly flat with staying, especially once you account for the Meta bonus and unvested stock I'd forfeit. To make this a clear yes, I'd need a base of $260K, a GSU grant of $1.35M, and a $100K sign-on to cover what I'm leaving behind. If we can get close to that, I'm ready to sign."

**Don't invent a competing offer.** "I'm happy where I am" is true, and it's strong leverage on its own.

## How to decide

- **Accept** if they get you to roughly $600K+ averaged over four years, plus a meaningful sign-on.
- **Probably stay** if they barely move. On pay alone, ~$26K/yr more with lower years 3–4 isn't much reason to give up a job you like. That's especially true since it means restarting your track record, and future refreshes, from zero at a new company.

One more question to ask the recruiter: how Google's refresh grants vest, and what a typical refresh is for an L6 PM who meets expectations. That's the biggest unknown for years 3–4.

content.text:
**Yes. On pay alone, this is worth taking.** They fixed the two problems with the first offer: your base is now no longer below what you make today, and the money you'd forfeit at Meta is covered. Pushing further on the money probably won't get you much more. Before you sign, sort out two things: your start date and the sign-on repayment terms.

## The final offer next to staying at Meta

This assumes Google's front-loaded vesting schedule, which Levels.fyi lists as
38% in year 1, 32% in year 2, 20% in year 3, 10% in year 4

. It also assumes the sign-on is paid in year 1 and Google gives you **no** refresh grants.

| | Google | Meta | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year 1 | $898K ($288K cash + $410K stock + $200K sign-on) | $476K | **+$422K** |
| Year 2 | $634K | $526K | **+$108K** |
| Year 3 | $504K | $526K | −$22K |
| Year 4 | $396K | $526K | −$130K |
| **4-year total** | **$2.43M (~$608K/yr)** | **$2.05M (~$514K/yr)** | **+$378K** |

That's about $94K/yr more, up from $26K/yr in the first offer. It also meets the bar I suggested last time: around $600K+ a year averaged over four years, plus a meaningful sign-on. If the stock instead vests evenly at 25% a year, the 4-year total doesn't change; only the year-by-year timing does.

**The catch:** years 3–4 are still below Meta unless Google gives you refresh grants, and the recruiter said those aren't guaranteed. Most of your advantage comes in years 1–2. Even if you got no refreshes at all, you'd still be about $378K ahead after four years. My Meta numbers assume you keep getting refreshes there, so this comparison leans toward staying, not toward Google.

## Before you sign

**1. Time your resignation around Meta's November 15 vest. It's 11 days away.**
Meta's four quarterly vest dates are February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15.

At about $200K over the next 12 months, the next vest is worth roughly $50K. Don't give notice until it has landed in your account, and set your Google start date after it. Also check when your next Meta bonus pays out. If it's close, ask for a start date after that too. Recruiters often agree to start-date requests even after saying "best offer," because it costs Google nothing.

**2. Read the sign-on repayment terms.**
The most common time periods he sees are one to two years.
Some contracts require you to pay back the full amount and some only a prorated share. Also note that
resigning before the clawback period ends could mean repaying the gross bonus rather than the amount you actually received after taxes

, meaning the pre-tax amount, not what you actually took home. Ask how long the repayment period is, whether it's prorated, and whether the $200K comes as one payment or is split across years. A $200K sign-on effectively ties you to Google for a while, so make sure you're comfortable with that.

**3. Get everything in writing:** the vesting schedule and how often shares vest, the sign-on terms, and your level (L6).

## Decision

- **Take it** if you're genuinely excited about the role and comfortable staying at least as long as the repayment period. You come out about $378K ahead over four years even if Google never gives you a refresh.
- **Stay** if the main draw was money and you're uneasy about years 3–4. In that case you'd be giving up a job you like mostly for a front-loaded payout.

Since you said compensation matters a lot to you, I'd take it. Just accept with a start date after November 15, and after your Meta bonus if it's close.

One correction to my last message: I gave figures like the ~$607K L6 median as if they were confirmed, but I hadn't checked them. Treat those as rough benchmarks. The vesting schedule above is from Levels.fyi, but confirm your actual schedule with the recruiter.
